name: Dial-up
web: Modems and BBSes, HyperCard, then the hand-built page: HTML tables, view source, PHP3 and MySQL by 1999.

opens.event: The World Wide Web is announced to the public on alt.hypertext

intro.html: I was an “Arty Kid” and a “Computery Kid,” and I loved computers when I was a kid: they were clearly tools for making art. I took my first coding class at a public school when I was 12, at a computer-math-science magnet school in San Diego. By 1999 I’d click “view source” in my browser, copy out some of their clever HTML code, and learn from their ideas, and when Spiremedia posted for a receptionist, my email’s subject line said “I don’t want to be your receptionist.” The night of July 7th, 2000, I couldn’t sleep, so I took the main data points of my day and codified them into an XML/HTML-type language.

name: Broadband
web: Flash against the standards movement, blogging, AJAX in 2005, Web 2.0.

intro.html: Then something funny happened that we weren’t expecting, but sort of hoping for: the web became a tool everyone used, all the time, for a ton of reasons. I spent those years being unemployed, doing lots of freelance, building a web page with only 5 kilobytes of code, and building custom Content Management Systems in PHP every time I launched a website for a client. In September 2005, I was 26 years old, and I was about to spend 4 years at a company in Boulder called Wall Street on Demand.

name: Apps
web: The iPhone and the App Store, Twitter, the Facebook platform, the cloud, the Quantified Self.

intro.html: I spent 6 months designing a 15×10 GIF (among many other things) for the front page of the New York Times, and by late 2007 I oversaw 60-70% of the design and front-end engineering work. Then I got a job at Automattic, working on the blogging system I was using to publish my posts. I discovered I had been developing an often-messy and laborious but enjoyable and endlessly-evolving process of designing and coding web interface functionality directly in the browser.

name: Design systems
web: React, npm and Node everywhere, design systems as a job, Next.js and Vercel, TypeScript.

opens.event: React is released as open source at JSConf US

intro.html: In September 2014, I organized a workshop for four designers to bring Calypso into a more pure Atomic Design model, then created and edited core Calypso components to carry it across the entire app. When Automattic released Calypso’s source after the better part of two years, I couldn’t be prouder. At CA, I took Material UI and customized it for our needs, my first introduction to TypeScript; at Community Funded, React and Next.js were my suggestions, and we launched to live clients in the first quarter of 2020.

name: Agents
web: Large language models, coding agents, the Model Context Protocol, agentic development.

intro.html: In March my team at Cisco was told it was turning entirely to agentic development, and I chose that moment to start working with Claude. I now run all three of our teams. At Cisco the work is the design system and the people who build with it: opening it to agents, putting agents on a schedule with guardrails, and running three teams with a system that drafts while I decide. At home it's the same way of working on things I care about: a motorsport information system for my racing rig, tracks built from real roads, an open protocol for how AI should talk to people, and this site.
